methods.label: Triangles from the common center
methods.explanation:
The repeated rotations suggest dividing the covered region into equal pieces. Let \(O\) be the common center. A \(30^\circ\) rotation permutes the three squares, because turning a square through \(90^\circ\) leaves it unchanged. Their twelve corners are therefore spaced \(30^\circ\) apart around \(O\).

Each square corner is exposed: it is \(3\sqrt2\) from \(O\), and another square reaches that distance only at its own, differently located corners. Since the outline has 24 sides, rotational symmetry gives exactly one inward vertex between each consecutive pair of square corners.

Let \(V,W\) be consecutive outer corners, and let \(Q\) be the inward vertex between them. Let \(M\) be the midpoint of the side of \(V\)'s square that contains the boundary edge \(VQ\). Then \(OM=MV=3\) and \(OM\perp MV\), so \(\angle MOV=45^\circ\). Reflection in the bisector of \(\angle VOW\) preserves the arrangement and interchanges \(V\) and \(W\). It fixes \(Q\), giving
\[
\angle VOQ=15^\circ,
\qquad \angle MOQ=45^\circ-15^\circ=30^\circ.
\]
In the right triangle \(OMQ\), write \(MQ=x>0\). The side opposite \(30^\circ\) is half the hypotenuse, so \(OQ=2x\). The Pythagorean theorem gives
\[
3^2+x^2=(2x)^2,
\qquad x=\sqrt3.
\]
Thus \(Q\) lies between \(M\) and \(V\), and
\[
VQ=MV-MQ=3-\sqrt3.
\]
Rotations carry each pair of boundary edges to the next pair, and reflection through an outer corner interchanges its two edges. Hence all 24 edges have this length. Each edge lies on a square side, whose perpendicular distance from \(O\) is 3.

Every square contains \(O\), so the covered region meets each ray from \(O\) in one unbroken segment. Joining \(O\) to the boundary vertices therefore partitions the region into 24 triangles without gaps or overlapping interiors. Its area is
\[
24\cdot\frac12\cdot(3-\sqrt3)\cdot3
=108-36\sqrt3.
\]
Since 3 is squarefree, \(a=108\), \(b=36\), and \(c=3\). Therefore \(a+b+c=147\), choice \(\boxed{\text{E}}\).
